column2: The assembly members should know dharma; the scribe skilled in letters; the door-keepers should be well-disposed and know the times for summoning.
The treasury head should know gems and the like; a man beneficial at the gate; a physician knowing Ayurveda; the elephant-chief and one knowing horses and the like;
an elephant-rider who has conquered fatigue; the horse-chief like the elephant one; the fort-chief beneficial and wise; the architect knowing Vastu-science;
the master of weapons, skilled in released-by-machine, released-by-hand, unreleased and held-released weapons and in wrestling, is beneficial to the king.
An old man should head the inner palace; women of fifty years and men of seventy should move about in all tasks;
one should be vigilant in the armory; having known, livelihood is arranged. The king, knowing works as best, worst and middling,
should appoint men as best, worst and middling. A king wishing to conquer the earth should have allies, wise and beneficial:
the righteous in works of dharma, the brave in battle, the skilled in matters of wealth, and everywhere the pure;
he should appoint eunuchs among women, and the sharp in harsh deeds. A man known to the king as pure in any matter,
he should employ in dharma, wealth and desire; the lowest in lowest things; the king should act fittingly with those tested by tests.
With counsel, as is just, he should make the elephant-forest-rangers; in seeking their trail he should appoint diligent superintendents.
In whatever work one has skill, in that he should be employed; he should employ servants of his father and grandfather in all works,
except in matters of heirs, for they have gathered there. People who have come from another king's house seeking refuge,
whether wicked or not, one should receive carefully; knowing one wicked he should not trust him, but keep him under control.
Those who have come from other countries, having known them by spies at his side, he should honor. Enemies are like a fire-rain, a snake, a sword together;
servants and bad servants are to be known likewise. The king should have spies as eyes and should always appoint spies:
mild, unnoticed by the people and unknown to each other, merchants skilled in counsel, astrologers, physicians,
and those with the form of renunciants, discerning strength and weakness. The king should not trust one; he should trust many reports.
The affection and disaffection of servants and the virtues and faults of people, of good and bad, one should know for control.
One should do deeds that produce affection and avoid those that produce disaffection; by prosperity beloved of the people the king is a pleaser of the people.
The subjects who are being devoured are to be protected, especially from clerks; protected from their fear, those subjects are the king's.
Unprotected, they become the food of those same people here. One should crush the wicked and take the tax prescribed in the scriptures;
one should put half into the treasury and always give half to a Brahmin. A best Brahmin finding a treasure may take it all;
a quarter, an eighth, a sixteenth — a twice-born should give in order of castes the treasure to a worthy person by dharma.
One speaking falsely should be fined an eighth of his good wealth. Property whose owner is lost the king should deposit for three years;
before three years the owner may take it; after, the king takes it. One who says "this is mine," in accordance with rule,
having established the form, number and so on, the owner deserves that property. The king should protect the property of a minor heir
until he has returned or until childhood is past. So too for the minor-son women and the childless,
for chaste women, widows and the afflicted. Those relatives who seize the property of these while living,
the righteous king should punish with a thief's punishment. What is carried off by thieves in general the king himself should restore;
the king too may recover what was taken from those charged with guarding against thieves. One who claims theft where none was taken should be expelled and fined;
the king should not give what was taken by household members in the house. The king should take a twentieth of goods from his own country, twice-born;
the toll portion from other countries, making known loss and expense; having known, he should fix the toll so the merchant gets profit;
he should take a twentieth of profit; otherwise he is to be punished. One should avoid ferry-tolls on women and renunciants;
in ferries, loss through the fault of servants the servants should make good. A sixth of bearded grains, an eighth of pod grains,
the king should take for the forest, according to place and time. A fifth or sixth the king should take of animals and gold;
of scents, herbs and juices, of flowers, roots and fruits, of leaves, vegetables and grass, of bamboo, cane and hides,
of split things and vessels and everything made of stone — a sixth he should take, and of honey, meat and ghee.
Even dying he should not take a tax from Brahmins. In whose king's land a Shrotriya suffers from hunger,
that kingdom suffers from disease, famine and thieves. Having known his learning and conduct, he should arrange his livelihood;
he should protect him on all sides like a father an own son. Protected by the king, whoever does dharma daily,
by that the king's life, wealth and kingdom increase. Craftsmen should do one month's work for the king,
and others who live by their own bodies, with only a meal in return.
One who wipes her face when kissed, does not value what is given, who sleeps first even though asleep and wakes later,
who shakes her limbs when touched and holds back her body, who hears even pleasing words slightly, turning away,
who does not look at what is offered in front, and hides her hips, whose face goes pale when seen, who turns away from his friends,
and appears indifferent among the women who desire him, who knowing the time for adornment does not adorn herself —
such a woman is disaffected; leaving her one should approach an affectionate woman. One who is glad at the sight, who turns away when looked at,
who when watched casts a restless glance elsewhere, yet cannot altogether turn away,
who reveals her own private limbs, Bhargava, and carefully hides a blameworthy limb,
who at seeing him embraces and kisses a girl, who when spoken to becomes truthful in speech,
who when touched has her limbs thrilled and is enjoyed with sweat, and who, Rama, asks for easily obtained things,
then having obtained even a little is greatly glad, who rejoices at hearing his name recited and values it much,
who sends him fruits marked with nail-marks, and places what he sent in her heart with respect,
who with embraces anoints her limbs as if with nectar, who sleeps when he sleeps first and wakes with him,
who touches the thighs excessively and wakes the sleeping man — [now perfumes:] with powder of kapittha and a garland of curds,
ghee becomes fragrant, with milk added and barley. The preparation of food thus; the release of scent is shown.
Cleansing, rinsing, Rama, and likewise purging, steeping and cooking, awakening, fumigating,
and perfuming are directed: this is remembered as the eightfold set of operations. With leaves of kapittha, bilva, jambu, mango and oleander,
making water, the substance cleansed is the cleansing; in their absence cleansing is by musk-water.
Nail-perfume, kushtha, ghana, mamsi, sprikka, shaileya-born water, likewise saffron, lac, sandal, agaru, nirada,
sarala, devakashtha, camphor with kanta, bala, kundurukka, guggulu, Shrinivasaka,
with sarjarasa — thus twenty-one incense substances. From this group of twenty-one incense substances, at will,
taking two substances each one should join them with portions of sarja; joined with nakha, pinyaka, malaya and honey,
incense compounds are made here as desired. Bark, nadi, fruit, oil, saffron, granthi, pravartaka,
shaileya, tagara, kranta, chola, camphor, mamsi, spirit and kushtha — one should direct as bath substances.
Taking three substances from these at will, a bath with musk is to be made, increasing desire.
With bark, mura, anala and nada in equal parts, with half of bala, the bath would be lotus-scented; with oil it resembles saffron;
joined with half of tagara it would be jasmine-fragrant; with sadhyamaka, like vakula in scent, charming;
having placed manjishtha, tagara, chola, bark, tiger-claw, nakkha and gandhapatra, a good scented oil would result.
Oil pressed, Rama, from sesame scented with flowers becomes by perfuming surely like the flower in scent.
Cardamom, clove, kakkola, nutmeg, camphor, with mace — these are independent mouth-perfumes.
Camphor, saffron, kanta, musk, harenuka, kakkola, cardamom and clove, jati and kosha,
bark-leaf, truti and mustaka, lata and musk, the thorns of clove, fruit and leaf of jati,
and the pungent fruit, Rama, one should prepare in karsha measures; in their powder one should add the essence of khadira, a fourth, perfumed.
